title: Stonehenge Altar Stone: Origin Still a Mystery
paragraphs: The Altar Stone at Stonehenge, a sandstone slab roughly 4.9 metres long and weighing about six tons, has puzzled researchers for decades. For almost a century the prevailing view was that it came from west Wales, as the smaller bluestones did. Earlier research then pointed instead to north-east Scotland, which would have meant a far longer journey; by comparison, the bluestones travelled about 225 kilometres.

A new study in the Journal of the Geological Society, led by Professor Duncan Pirrie of the University of South Wales, has put the Scottish theory to the test. The team combined fresh observations of the monument with analysis of fragments held in museum collections, examining the stone's structure, mineral content, chemical composition and isotopic signatures to build a geological fingerprint. This was then compared with rock formations such as those of the Orcadian Basin.

The outcome is a puzzle rather than an answer. "So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone," Pirrie said. The results eliminate several possibilities but do not disprove a Scottish source, and the stone's true origin remains unidentified. As one co-author put it, each location ruled out narrows the search.

questions.q: How far did the bluestones travel?
How did the team build a 'geological fingerprint'?
questions.a: By examining structure, minerals, chemistry and isotopes.

questions.q: What do the results not prove?
questions.a: That a Scottish source is impossible.
